title: Learning the shape of a slower week
excerpt: A few mornings offline, a new sketchbook, and more time noticing what the work is asking for.
body:
I left the laptop closed until ten this morning. Tea, a short walk, then three pages in the sketchbook before opening a file.

The surprise was not a new idea. It was noticing that the question I had been trying to answer was not the question the project needed. The team did not need another flow. We needed to agree on what a patient should know before they arrived.

A slower start made room for a more useful conversation. Keeping that in the week.

title: The quiet work of removing things
excerpt: Good product design often arrives one subtraction at a time. A note on restraint, confidence, and knowing when the interface is done.
body:
On a recent project, we spent a week making a dashboard feel more useful. We added summaries, clarified the hierarchy, and tried a different navigation. None of it addressed the feeling that there was too much to hold in your head.

The change that helped was removing a panel. It repeated information the person already knew, but in language that made them stop and check. Taking it away did not remove a capability. It removed a small demand on attention.

This is the less visible part of the work. You have to understand a system well enough to distinguish what supports a decision from what merely describes the database. That takes conversations, observation, and a willingness to throw away something you have already made.

My test now is simple: if this disappeared, what would become harder? If the answer is difficult to name, I try the version without it. Not because less is always better, but because every element asks for a little trust. It should earn its place.

title: What prototypes are actually for
excerpt: Not tiny versions of the final thing. They are questions made tangible enough for a team to answer together.
body:
The most useful prototype I made last month had six screens, no working navigation, and a note where the hard part should have been. It answered the question we needed to answer in twenty minutes.

We were not testing whether someone could complete a task. We were testing whether a clinical team understood a handover in the same way. Putting a specific example in front of people made the difference in their assumptions visible.

A prototype needs enough fidelity to make its question real, and no more. Sometimes that means code and realistic data. Sometimes it means a printed page with room to write on it. The tool matters less than the conversation it makes possible.

Before I open a file, I write one sentence: what would we do differently depending on what we learn? If I cannot finish that sentence, I am probably polishing rather than prototyping.
